easy.heading: Warming Up With a Simple Chain Reaction
easy.body:
I started today by looking for the easiest entry point, which was the empty cell at [3,0]. In this puzzle, empty means zero pips. Looking at our available dominoes, only the [0,6] pair fit that description. So, I placed the zero at [3,0] and the six at [3,1]. This was a huge help because [3,1] was part of an equals region with [2,1], meaning [2,1] had to be a six too.

To finish off the bottom of the board, I looked for a domino that had a six to pair with that [2,1] spot. The [3,6] domino was the perfect candidate. Placing the six at [2,1] left me with a three at [2,2]. Since [2,2] and [1,2] were also marked as equal, I knew [1,2] had to be a three. From there, I used the [4,3] domino to fill [1,3] and [1,2], and the rest of the board just fell into place using the [4,4] and [1,1] pairs.

medium.heading: Navigating the Equals and Sums
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt a bit more crowded, but it followed a really logical path. I noticed the empty cell at [1,1] first. Since the only domino with a zero was [0,3], I knew [1,1] and its partner [0,1] had to be that pair. This put a zero in the empty spot and a three in [0,1]. Even though there was a less than constraint there, the zero and three combination worked once I saw how the neighbors connected.

I also spent some time on the left side where [2,0] had to be greater than 4. The [6,2] domino worked perfectly there, putting the six at [2,0] and the two at [2,1]. This then dictated that [2,2] and [3,2] also had to be twos because of the equals constraint. It is really all about finding those anchor points like the sum of 5 at [2,4] and letting the rest of the board fill itself in piece by piece.

hard.heading: Solving the Giant Equals Region
hard.body:
The hard puzzle today was a real test of patience, mostly because of that massive equals region. It linked six different cells together, including [2,3], [3,1], [3,2], [3,3], [4,1], and [5,1]. I realized I needed a pip value that appeared frequently in our domino list. By looking at dominoes like [3,3], [3,4], and [3,6], it became clear that the number three was the secret to unlocking that whole middle section.

Another tough spot was the sum of 15 in the top right. With cells [1,4], [1,5], and [2,4] needing to add up to 15, I knew I had to use some of the highest pips available. I used the [6,6] domino for a big chunk of that total. It took a few tries to get the orientation right for the [5,4] and [5,3] dominoes nearby, but once those high numbers were settled, the lower values like the [1,0] and [2,1] dominoes were much easier to slot in.

explanation.tips: When you are just starting out, always look for the empty cells or the sum regions with very high or very low targets first. These spots usually only have one or two possible dominoes that can fit, which gives you a great starting point for the rest of the grid. Also, try to keep a mental list of which dominoes you have already used so you don't get stuck trying to place a pair that is already on the board.
explanation.learned: Today I learned that those long equals regions are actually your best friends rather than something to be afraid of. They might look intimidating because they cover so many cells, but they actually narrow down your choices very quickly. I also realized how helpful it is to look at the total number of times a specific pip value appears in the domino list to solve those larger regions.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You solve Pips by placing a set of dominoes onto a grid so that they follow specific rules like sums, equal values, or greater than and less than constraints. Each domino can only be used once.

faqs.question: What does the equals sign mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An equals region means that every cell inside that shaded area must have the exact same number of pips, even if those cells belong to different dominoes.

faqs.question: What is an empty cell in the Pips game?
faqs.answer: An empty cell is a special constraint that requires the cell to have zero pips. This usually means you need to find a domino that has a blank side.

faqs.question: What are some good NYT Pips strategy tips?
faqs.answer: Start with the most restrictive areas first, like cells that must sum to a very high or very low number. Use the process of elimination by crossing off dominoes from your list as you place them.

faqs.question: How do sum constraints work in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum constraint identifies a group of cells that must add up to a specific total. You have to figure out which domino values can be placed in those specific spots to reach that exact sum.
